title: Bede
hook: a monk who wrote a history of the English church and died finishing a translation

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cuthbert, and a secret kept. Your line was the sea and the otters. Who did you warm up? Day seven hundred ninety-four.

"Dear master, there's still one sentence not written." A boy is sitting with a pen in a monk's cell in the north of England. On the floor nearby, an old monk is dying, and he's short of breath. They've been working all day. The old man has been dictating, the boy writing, and they are nearly done. All week, one man has stood behind the stories: Hilda, Caedmon, Cuthbert, Augustine and the temples. This dying monk wrote them down. His name is Bede. Today, the storyteller himself, and the last sentence.

Bede tells us a little about himself at the end of his history of the English church. He was given to the monastery as a child and spent his whole life there, at Wearmouth and Jarrow. His delight, he says, was always in learning, or teaching, or writing. He wrote in Latin, the language of scholars, and he wrote a great deal: on scripture, on time and the calendar, on the saints, and the history we've been reading from all week. His death comes to us in a letter from one of his students, a monk named Cuthbert, not the Cuthbert of the otters. In his last days, the letter says, Bede was translating the Gospel of John into English. He got as far as a verse in chapter six. A boy has a little food, and Andrew asks Jesus, "but what are they among so many?" He also stopped, the letter says, to hand out a few small things he owned, a little pepper, some cloth, some incense, to the priests of the house. Then the boy, Wilberht, says it. Dear master, one sentence left. Bede says: write it quickly. A moment later: it's finished. And Bede answers, you've spoken truly, it is finished. They are the words Jesus says from the cross in John's Gospel. Bede asks to be held, facing the place where he used to pray, and he dies on the floor of his cell, singing the old words of praise: glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. A whole life of work, and the last sentence still mattered.

Here's the practice: finish one sentence you started. Settle, and breathe. Think of something small you left half-done. An email sitting in drafts. A text you began and never sent. A thank-you note. A line in a journal. A sentence you started saying to someone and swallowed. Choose just one. If you can, finish it now, while the bell holds, and then put the pen or the phone down and breathe. If it has to wait, decide the exact words in your head. If you pray, you can offer the small work to God. If you don't, simply let it be done. The bell holds the time.
Bede. The monk of Jarrow who wrote the history we've been reading, and died translating John's Gospel, one sentence from the end.
Your line: finish the work. Today, send or say the sentence you finished. Then say to yourself, quietly, it is finished. Day seven hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Catholics and Anglicans honor the Venerable Bede as a saint, and Catholics count him a Doctor of the Church; his history is still read by students of the early English church.

notes: The index hook said 'wrote the first history of England'; per the claims rule the hook field and script say 'a history of the English church'. Confirm.
Bede 5.24: given to the monastery as a child (he says aged seven; the age is left out), lifelong at Wearmouth–Jarrow, delight in learning, teaching, writing. Paraphrased; confirm.

Cuthbert's Letter on the Death of Bede: John translated into English up to 6:9; gifts of pepper, napkins (orarios) and incense; Wilberht's 'one sentence'; 'consummatum est'; dying on the floor of his cell singing the Gloria. Paraphrased; confirm, including whether he was 'held' facing his place of prayer.
John 6:9 in the KJV is spoken by Andrew (6:8–9); confirm the attribution in the script.
'glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit' is the doxology Bede sang, given here descriptively (not quoted from a translation); confirm.
